title: What is & How to Do Memoization
description: Turn slow recursion into fast top-down DP by caching subproblem results

sections.title: 4. How to Add Memoization Step by Step
7. How to Approach a Problem with Memoization

blocks.text: Memoization is the gentlest way into dynamic programming. You write the natural recursive solution, then add one small thing: a cache that remembers answers you have already computed. That single change can turn an exponential solution into a fast one.
Because you start from plain recursion, memoization is often called the top-down approach. You begin with the big problem and let recursion break it down.
Memoization means storing the result of a function call so that if you ever call it again with the same input, you return the saved answer instead of computing it a second time.
It only helps when the same subproblem appears many times. That property is called overlapping subproblems, and it is exactly what dynamic programming problems have.

items: Solve a problem recursively as you normally would
Before computing, check if the answer is already cached
If yes, return it instantly
If no, compute it once and store it for next time

blocks.text: Take Fibonacci, where fib(n) equals fib(n-1) plus fib(n-2). The plain recursion looks clean, but it is painfully slow.
Look at the call tree. The same subproblems appear over and over, which is why the work explodes exponentially.

blocks.caption: fib(2) and other subproblems are recomputed many times in plain recursion

blocks.text: This tree has enormous repetition. The count of calls roughly doubles at each level, giving O(2^n) time. Memoization removes every repeated branch.
We keep a cache, often an array or a hash map, indexed by the function input. Before doing any real work, we look in the cache. After computing, we store the result.

blocks.caption: Check the cache first, compute only on a miss, then store the result

blocks.text: Now every distinct subproblem is solved exactly once. With n distinct inputs, the whole thing runs in O(n).

content.title: 4. How to Add Memoization Step by Step

blocks.text: The beauty of memoization is that you barely change your recursion. Follow these steps.

items: Write the correct recursive solution first, with its base cases.
Create a cache sized to the range of inputs, filled with a sentinel like -1 for not computed.
At the top of the function, if the cache already holds this input, return it.
Just before returning, store the computed answer in the cache.

blocks.text: Here is Fibonacci again, now memoized. Notice how little changed.

codes.python:
def fib(n, memo):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    if memo[n] != -1:                         # cache hit
        return memo[n]
    memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo)  # compute once, store
    return memo[n]

blocks.text:
Two lines is all it takes:

A cache check at the top and a cache store at the bottom. The rest of your recursion stays exactly the same.
Memoization shines in specific situations. Reach for it when the following are true.

items: You can already picture the recursive solution clearly.
The same subproblems repeat, so caching actually saves work.
The set of distinct inputs is small enough to store.
Only some of the state space is actually reached, so top-down avoids wasted cells.

blocks.text: That last point is a real advantage. Top-down only ever computes the subproblems it truly needs, while bottom-up fills every cell whether used or not.
Memoization is easy, but a few traps catch beginners.

items: Recursion depth: very deep recursion can overflow the call stack.
Cache key: the key must capture the full state, or you will return wrong cached answers.
Sentinel clash: pick a not computed marker that can never be a real answer.
Multiple parameters: with two changing inputs you need a 2D cache, not a 1D one.

content.title: 7. How to Approach a Problem with Memoization

blocks.text: When you meet a new DP problem, memoization is usually the fastest path to a first correct solution.

items: Describe the answer recursively in terms of smaller inputs.
Nail the base cases so the recursion terminates.
Add a cache keyed by the exact state the function depends on.
Return early on a cache hit and store before every return.
If it works but recursion depth worries you, convert it to tabulation next.

blocks.text: Get memoization working first. It is the clearest way to prove your recurrence is correct before you optimise further.
